power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 3 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: There was no evidence against proportional hazards for FPC2 (p ≥ 0.63).
Faded estimates: p ≥ 0.05. individuals at elevated risk and to tailor interventions to their daily activity patterns.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≥ 0.63", "p ≥ 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05" ), Sentence = c("There was no evidence against proportional hazards for FPC2 (p ≥ 0.63).", "Faded estimates: p ≥ 0.05.", "Faded estimates: p ≥ 0.05. individuals at elevated risk and to tailor interventions to their daily activity patterns." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 19 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:19, File = c("1_data_hip.R", "1_data_wrist.R", 
"2_1_data_explore.R", "2_2_Cosinor_analysis.R", "3_Residual_(m)fpca_plots.R", 
"3_Residual_(m)fpca.R", "4_1_data_prep.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", "4_3_FPC2_robustness.R", 
"5_1_mfpca_level2.R", "5_2_Eigenfunction_interpretation.R", "6_1_Toolbox_Clustering.R", 
"6_2_Toolbox_mortality_prediction.R", "6_3_Toolbox.R", "build_reference.R", 
"deploy_shinyapps.R", "helpers.R", "app.R", "run_cluster_tool.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", 
"—", "4_1_data_prep.R, 1_data_wrist.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", 
"4_2_FPC2.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", "4_2_FPC2.R, 6_2_Toolbox_mortality_prediction.R", 
"4_2_FPC2.R, 6_1_Toolbox_Clustering.R, 6_3_Toolbox.R, 6_2_Toolbox_mortality_prediction.R", 
"—", "—", "build_reference.R, helpers.R", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "none", "none", "dependency", 
"none")), row.names = c(NA, -19L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `Shiny_tool/logo` to `logo` (in deploy_shinyapps.R); `Shiny_tool/examples` to `examples` (in deploy_shinyapps.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **12 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `paxmin_g.xpt`, `paxmin_h.xpt`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 19 scripts: 0 ran without error, 13 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts need a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: app.R, run_cluster_tool.R. Naming the file in the script solves this.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("1_data_hip.R", "1_data_wrist.R", "2_1_data_explore.R", 
"2_2_Cosinor_analysis.R", "3_Residual_(m)fpca_plots.R", "3_Residual_(m)fpca.R", 
"4_1_data_prep.R", "4_2_FPC2.R", "4_3_FPC2_robustness.R", "5_1_mfpca_level2.R", 
"5_2_Eigenfunction_interpretation.R", "6_1_Toolbox_Clustering.R", 
"6_2_Toolbox_mortality_prediction.R", "6_3_Toolbox.R", "build_reference.R", 
"deploy_shinyapps.R", "helpers.R", "app.R", "run_cluster_tool.R"
), Outcome = c("dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable", 
"errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", "dependency_unavailable", 
"errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", 
"errored", "errored", "run_by_source", "needs_a_person", "needs_a_person"
), Detail = c("dependency_unavailable", "dependency_unavailable", 
"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "dependency_unavailable", 
"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime", 
"runtime", "runtime", "", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(1.3, 1.3, 2.4, 
2.5, 2.1, 3.1, 1.7, 2.8, 2.7, 2.8, 2.2, 3.3, 2.9, 3.7, 2.6, 1.1, 
0, 0, 0)), row.names = c(NA, -19L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("1_data_hip.R", "1_data_wrist.R", "4_2_FPC2.R"
)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

7 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**Run by another script**

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "helpers.R", "Run by" = "app.R"), row.names = "helpers.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

info.title: Beyond the 24-Hour Rhythm: Functional Principal Components of Daily Activity Residuals and Mortality in NHANES

author.affiliation:
Public and Occupational Health
								Amsterdam UMC location Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
								
									1117
									De Boelelaan Amsterdam
									the Netherlands

text.text: Background.
Accelerometer-derived 24-hour activity profiles are usually summarised by cosinor rhythm parameters or by functional principal component analysis (FPCA).
Applied to the raw profiles, however, the leading functional components largely reexpress what the cosinor already captures: activity level, rhythm strength and timing.
Whether the shape of the day carries health information beyond these parameters is unclear.
Methods.

We analysed adults with seven valid days of accelerometry from two National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohorts: hip activity counts (2003)(2004)(2005)(2006); n = 2,615) and wrist Monitor-Independent Movement Summary units (2011-2014; n = 3,208).
Minute-level activity was transformed with the inverse hyperbolic sine, and a single 24-hour cosinor curve was fitted across each participant's seven days.
Each participant's average residual curve, which contains no 24-hour component, was decomposed by FPCA and, to separate stable between-person patterns from day-to-day variation, by multilevel FPCA.
In exploratory analyses, we related the three leading components to all-cause mortality and, secondarily, to cardiovascular and cancer mortality.
We used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, income and the cosinor parameters, with the hip cohort for discovery and the wrist cohort for replication.
Results.
The three leading residual components explained 44% (hip) and 51% (wrist) of residual variance and consisted mainly of 12-hour and 8-hour patterns.
The second component (FPC2) contrasts an early-starting, flat day with a day of distinct midmorning and evening peaks.
Its shape was nearly identical in the two cohorts (similarity 0.96), and multilevel FPCA recovered it as a stable between-person pattern.

In unweighted models, FPC2 was the only component associated with all-cause mortality in the discovery cohort (hazard ratio per SD 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.29; Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.008), and the association replicated in the wrist cohort (1.18, 1.03 to 1.35; p = 0.017).

With survey weights that also accounted for selection into the analytic sample, the association was concentrated in cardiovascular deaths (hip 1.53, 1.12 to 2.09, p = 0.007; wrist 1.38, 1.10 to 1.72, p = 0.005).
This association persisted after further adjustment for lifestyle factors and traditional activity metrics.
FPC2 was not associated with cancer mortality.

Scores of the leading components did not form distinct clusters (average silhouette width ≤ 0.23), but FPC2 was selected as a continuous predictor of cardiovascular mortality in both cohorts by forward selection on 10-fold cross-validated, survey-weighted AUC.
Conclusions.
The within-day structure of activity that a 24-hour cosinor cannot represent varies continuously between people.
One replicated aspect of it, the loss of a two-peak daily pattern, was associated with mortality beyond rhythm strength and timing, most clearly cardiovascular mortality.
The shape of daily activity therefore carries prognostic information beyond standard rhythm summaries.
It can support mortality risk prediction that needs only a few personal details, and may help identify individuals at elevated risk and tailor interventions to their daily activity patterns.
Accelerometers now record human movement continuously over 24 hours in large population studies, including the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) and the UK Biobank [1, 2].
text.formatted: Accelerometers now record human movement continuously over 24 hours in large population studies, including the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) and the UK Biobank <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Each participant contributes several days of high-resolution data, yet most epidemiological studies reduce these recordings to scalar summaries such as total activity or minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA).

Functional data analysis (FDA) offers an alternative: by modelling the 24-hour PA profile as a continuous function of time-of-day, it analyses the whole day as a smooth curve [3], accounting for the ordering of the measurements and their temporal correlation [4, 5].
text.formatted: Functional data analysis (FDA) offers an alternative: by modelling the 24-hour PA profile as a continuous function of time-of-day, it analyses the whole day as a smooth curve <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, accounting for the ordering of the measurements and their temporal correlation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: An early example is the functional linear model of Wang et al. [6], who represented averaged activity profiles with a nine-term Fourier basis and related them to sleep apnoea.
text.formatted: An early example is the functional linear model of Wang et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, who represented averaged activity profiles with a nine-term Fourier basis and related them to sleep apnoea.

text.text: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) has become the most widely used FDA tool for accelerometer data [7, 8].
text.formatted: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) has become the most widely used FDA tool for accelerometer data <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Applied to 24-hour activity profiles, it identifies a small number of dominant components of variation.
In older men in the MrOS study, the first four components predicted changes in sleep, cognition and mortality [9].
text.formatted: In older men in the MrOS study, the first four components predicted changes in sleep, cognition and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: In NHANES 2011-2014, Xiao et al. [10] identified four patterns in U.S. adults, interpreted as high amplitude, early rise, a prolonged activity window and a bi-phasic pattern, and related them to sociodemographic factors and self-rated health; a companion analysis applied the same approach to U.S. adolescents [11].
text.formatted: In NHANES 2011-2014, Xiao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> identified four patterns in U.S. adults, interpreted as high amplitude, early rise, a prolonged activity window and a bi-phasic pattern, and related them to sociodemographic factors and self-rated health; a companion analysis applied the same approach to U.S. adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Because accelerometer data have a nested structure, with days within participants, multilevel FPCA was introduced to separate variation between participants from day-to-day variation within participants [12, 13].
text.formatted: Because accelerometer data have a nested structure, with days within participants, multilevel FPCA was introduced to separate variation between participants from day-to-day variation within participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: It has since been extended to joint estimation with covariates [14] and to non-Gaussian data, including a generalized multilevel FPCA for binary active/inactive profiles in NHANES [15].
text.formatted: It has since been extended to joint estimation with covariates <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> and to non-Gaussian data, including a generalized multilevel FPCA for binary active/inactive profiles in NHANES <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: In addition, functional regression models link the functional representation curves to covariates or outcomes, either with the curve as response or as predictor [16, 17].
text.formatted: In addition, functional regression models link the functional representation curves to covariates or outcomes, either with the curve as response or as predictor <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17]</ref>.

text.text: Functional clustering groups participants with similar curves into phenotypes [18, 19], an approach that is attractive for describing population heterogeneity and for communicating interpretable behavioral phenotypes to public users of wearable devices.
text.formatted: Functional clustering groups participants with similar curves into phenotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19]</ref>, an approach that is attractive for describing population heterogeneity and for communicating interpretable behavioral phenotypes to public users of wearable devices.

text.text: Clustering can also identify combinations of functional characteristics that are difficult to summarize using single components [20, 21].
text.formatted: Clustering can also identify combinations of functional characteristics that are difficult to summarize using single components <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">21]</ref>.

text.text: In parallel, chronobiology summarises the same recordings with a small set of rhythm parameters [22].
text.formatted: In parallel, chronobiology summarises the same recordings with a small set of rhythm parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref>.

text.text: The cosinor model [23, 24] describes the day by its rhythm-adjusted mean level (mesor), the strength of the day-night contrast (amplitude) and the timing of the peak (acrophase); these parameters are widely used to characterise the rest-activity rhythm [25, 26, 27].

text.text: The two traditions in modeling PA patterns have developed largely separately, yet they overlap more than is usually acknowledged.

The 24-hour-periodic Fourier basis used in FDA smoothing decomposes the day into the 24-hour component and its higher harmonics (periods of 12, 8, 6 hours and so on), and the 24-hour component is closely related to the cosinor model.
Consistent with this, Xiao et al. [31, 10] showed that the leading components of FPCA on 24-hour profiles largely re-express amplitude and acrophase.

text.text: Furthermore, the cosinor assumes a symmetric daily rhythm around its peak [28]which cannot independently represent, for example, different steepness of the morning and evening transitions.

text.text: As a result, it remains unclear whether the functional representation carries health-relevant information beyond level, 24hour rhythm strength and timing, or whether it mainly re-expresses these parameters in a less interpretable form.
In this study we address this question directly by combining the two traditions in a decomposition that separates these features by construction.
For each participant, a cosinor model captures the typical level, rhythm strength and timing, and the residual curve captures the remaining shape of the day, which is then analysed by FPCA.
This yields shape components that do not overlap with the cosinor parameters.

Using two NHANES cohorts with different devices, hip-worn activity counts in 2003-2006 and wrist-worn MIMS units in 2011-2014, we (i) describe the main components of shape variation and their overlap with existing rhythm metrics, (ii) explore whether shape components are associated with all-cause mortality, and secondarily with cardiovascular and cancer mortality, beyond level, rhythm strength, timing and activity volume, and (iii) examine whether participants form distinct activity phenotypes by functional clustering.

Finally, we provide a web application in which users can upload their own accelerometer data and obtain the same decomposition, their shape score relative to the NHANES cohorts and their nearest activity group.
We used two NHANES cohorts.

In 2003-2006, participants wore a hip-worn accelerometer that recorded activity counts per minute; in 2011-2014, participants wore a wrist-worn accelerometer, and minute-level activity was summarised as Monitor-Independent Movement Summary (MIMS) units [34].

text.text: These parameters were used only to assess the overlap of shape with existing rhythm metrics and as additional adjustment; the residual shape was derived from the standard cosinor (2).
The participant's shape is the average residual ri (t) = 1 7 ∑︁ 7 j=1 r ij (t).

Let H = span{1, cos(ωt), sin(ωt)} and let P H be the orthogonal projection onto H. With complete, equally sampled days, the weekly fit equals the cosinor fit to the average day ȳi (t), so that ri = (I -P H ) ȳi (Supplementary Sections S1.2-S1.3).
The shape therefore has zero mean and no 24-hour component, and contains only the 12-hour and higher harmonics of the average day.
Level (M i ), rhythm (A i , ϕ i ) and shape (r i ) describe non-overlapping parts of each participant's average day, although they may be correlated across participants.
These properties hold exactly because all participants share the same design matrix X = [ 1, cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ], defined by a common time grid and a fixed 24-hour period.

The projection is thus identical for all participants, so every residual lies in the same space H ⊥ , as do the eigenfunctions estimated from all residuals in the FPCA below (Supplementary Section S1).

text.text: The participant shapes were decomposed as where µ(t) is the mean shape, φ k are orthonormal eigenfunctions of the covariance operator C r with eigenvalues λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ . . . , ξ ik are uncorrelated participant scores and ε i (t) is measurement error.

By (5), C r = (I -P H ) C ȳ (I -P H ), where C ȳ is the covariance operator of the average days, so every eigenfunction with a positive eigenvalue is orthogonal to the constant and to the 24-hour harmonic.

Residual FPCA is therefore not equivalent to FPCA of the activity curves with the leading components discarded, whose eigenfunctions can mix 24-hour and higher-harmonic variation (Supplementary Sections S1.4-S1.6).

Orthogonality holds for the eigenfunctions over time, not for the scores across participants: shape scores may still be associated with mesor, amplitude or acrophase (Supplementary Section S1.7), which we therefore included as covariates in the association analyses (Section 2.6.2).

The covariance was estimated with the fast covariance estimation (FACE) method [37], which smooths the covariance with penalised splines (penalty chosen by generalised crossvalidation) and removes the measurement-error contribution, using fpca.face in the R package refund; components were retained up to 90% of explained variance.

Each component was described by (i) the curves µ(t) ± 2 √ λ k φ k (t); (ii) the observed average day of participants scoring at least 1 SD above and at least 1 SD below the mean; (iii) the share of φ k at the 24-, 12-and 8-hour periods, as the R² from regressing φ k (t) on a cosine and sine of that period; and (iv) the similarity of the hip and wrist eigenfunctions, as the inner product of the normalised curves (1 = identical shape).

The projection was then multiplied by the FPCA shrinkage factor c k to give the score, which is the best linear predictor of ξ ik given p ik , and equals E(ξ ik | p ik ) when both are normally distributed.
The factor c k is a single constant for each component within a cohort, shared by all participants.

The mean µ, eigenfunction φ k , eigenvalue λ k and noise variance σ 2 were fixed at their estimates from the fitted cohort; no model was refitted.

To examine whether participants form distinct activity phenotypes, we applied k-means clustering to the FPCA scores of the participant-average asinh-transformed activity curves, retaining the components that together explain 90% of variance.
Scores were not standardized, so that k-means on the scores is equivalent to L 2 -based functional clustering of the projected curves.
The number of clusters K = 1, . . . , 8 was chosen by the gap statistic with the 1-SE rule, which can also indicate the absence of any cluster structure (K = 1).
Cluster separation was measured by the average silhouette width; values below 0.25 indicate no substantial cluster structure.
Level was represented by the cosinor mesor, rhythm strength by the cosinor amplitude, and timing by the acrophase, entered as the pair {cos(ωϕ i ), sin(ωϕ i )}.
Shape was represented by the standardised scores of the three leading residual components (FPC1-FPC3), a number fixed before the outcome analyses.

text.text: The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were cardiovascular and cancer mortality, analysed as cause-specific hazards with deaths from other causes censored.
Cox proportional hazards models included age, sex, ethnicity, family income, cosinor mesor, amplitude and acrophase (cosine and sine), and the three shape components jointly (Model 1).
Other covariates were included to adjust for potential confounding.
Proportional hazards were checked with scaled Schoenfeld residuals.
In a sensitivity analysis to reduce the potential influence of reverse causation, the analyses were repeated after excluding participants who died within the first two years of follow-up.
The hip cohort served as the discovery cohort and the wrist cohort as the replication cohort.

Testing was hierarchical: all three components were tested only for all-cause mortality in the discovery cohort, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction across FPC1-FPC3, and the component identified there was then tested alone in the replication cohort and for the secondary outcomes.

Because this component had the same shape and sign in both cohorts, its cohort-specific log hazard ratios were pooled descriptively by fixed-effect inverse-variance weighting, with heterogeneity assessed by Cochran's Q. Survey-weighted models were fitted with svycoxph in the R package survey [38], accounting for the sampling weights, strata and primary sampling units, and estimate associations for the US adult population.

As mentioned above, we conducted four sensitivity analyses: (i) comparing the FPCA components with the level-1 components of a multilevel FPCA, to rule out artifacts of day-to-day variation; (ii) excluding deaths in the first two years of follow-up, to reduce reverse causation; (iii) repeating all analyses in an expanded sample with less restrictive inclusion criteria; and (iv) adding lifestyle and functional variables to the candidate set for forward selection in the mortality prediction models..

text.text: FPC1 describes when the morning peak occurs: a sharp peak at about 7-8 am followed by an evening peak, against a later peak at about 10-11 am.
FPC2 describes whether the day has two peaks: high scores correspond to an early, slow start and a flat day, low scores to distinct mid-morning and evening peaks separated by an afternoon dip.
FPC3 describes three bursts of activity across the day.
As the correlation plot shows (Figure 3), the components were mostly not correlated with existing metrics.

text.text: The exception was FPC1, which correlated with the cosinor acrophase (Spearman ρ = -0.38 in the hip cohort and -0.65 in the wrist cohort) and with the extended cosinor width α (ρ = -0.45 and -0.24).
FPC2 correlated weakly with all of them.
The absolute correlations were at most 0.22 with the cosinor parameters, IS, IV, total activity and MVPA, and at most 0.27 with the extended cosinor parameters.
FPC2 therefore captures a pattern that the existing metrics do not.

text.text: Participants with high scores, the higher-risk end, were more active during night, started their day earlier (from about 4-6 am), lacked the mid-morning surge seen in the rest of the population and were less active in the evening.
Their median cosinor acrophase was 40 (hip) and 63 (wrist) minutes earlier than that of low scorers, and their IS significantly lower.
Participants with low scores rose sharply at about 7 am to a strong mid-morning peak at 9-10 am and remained active into the evening.

High scorers were less active overall than low scorers (189 versus 208 counts per minute, p = 0.003; 8.8 versus 10.2 MIMS units per minute, p < 0.001), although FPC2 was only weakly correlated with total activity (ρ = -0.11 and -0.21) and MVPA (-0.07 and -0.19).

text.text: In both cohorts, high scorers were more often male (38.0% versus 54.3% female in the hip cohort; 51.3% versus 69.2% in the wrist cohort).
In the hip cohort, high scorers were younger than low scorers and did not differ in income.
In the wrist cohort, the two groups did not differ in age, but high scorers more often had low income.
The pattern is therefore not explained by older age or lower income alone.
Both are adjusted for in the mortality models for FPC2 (Section 3.5).

Spearman correlations (Figure 3) among the variables of the mortality models show that total activity, MVPA and wear time were highly correlated with each other (ρ 0.88 to 0.97) and with the cosinor mesor (ρ up to 0.93); they were therefore added to Model 2 one at a time and not to Model 1.

text.text: In unweighted models with design-based standard errors (Figure 4), FPC2 remained associated with all-cause mortality in the hip discovery cohort (1.13 to 1.18), and the association was slightly stronger in the wrist replication cohort (1.17 to 1.25).

text.text: In survey-weighted models, the association of FPC2 with cardiovascular mortality was stable across adjustment sets (Figure 5).

text.text: Across the 12 specifications, hazard ratios ranged from 1.34 to 1.55 in the hip cohort and from 1.38 to 1.52 in the wrist cohort, and all were statistically significant.
In Model 2, which added the extended cosinor parameters, IS, IV, the circular SD of the acrophase and mobility difficulty, the hazard ratios were 1.43 (1.16 to 1.76) and 1.48 (1.13 to 1.94).
Further adjustment for wear time, MVPA, BMI, smoking, alcohol and education together gave 1.34 (1.03 to 1.75) and 1.50 (1.16 to 1.93).
All k-means fits converged.
The FPCA scores of the activity profiles (13 components explaining 91.6% and 91.8% of variance) did not form well-separated clusters.

The gap statistic selected K = 3 in the hip and K = 4 in the wrist cohort, but the average silhouette width was 0.20 and 0.18 for the selected solutions and at most 0.21 and 0.23 for any K from 2 to 8, below the 0.25 threshold for substantial structure throughout (Supplementary Figure S8).

text.text: Activity profiles therefore varied continuously between people, which supports the use of continuous component scores in health analyses.
The clusters, and their average 24-hour profiles (Figure 6), are provided in the interactive tool as descriptive groupings along this continuum, not as distinct phenotypes.

Without lifestyle and functional variables, the final models for predicting cardiovascular death were logit Pr(Y i = 1) = ⎧ ⎨ ⎩ β 0 + β 1 Age i + β ⊤ 2 Income i + β 3 Mesor i + β 4 Female i + β 5 FPC2 i , hip, where Income i is the vector of indicators for the income categories relative to the reference category.
Combined with the cosinor parameters and covariates, the score gives a predicted mortality risk from the final prediction model.
We developed a web application (https://quq-tot-orz.shinyapps.io/fpca-residual-tool/) in which users upload minute-level hip activity counts or wrist MIMS units, ideally for seven days.
text.formatted: We developed a web application (<ref type="url" target="https://quq-tot-orz.shinyapps.io/fpca-residual-tool/">https://quq-tot-orz.shinyapps.io/fpca-residual-tool/</ref>) in which users upload minute-level hip activity counts or wrist MIMS units, ideally for seven days.

text.text: The tool fits the cosinor, computes the residual shape and its FPC2 score from the fixed NHANES reference (mean, eigenfunction and FACE shrinkage factor), and reports the score in cohort SD units and percentiles alongside the mesor, amplitude and acrophase.

It also assigns the nearest descriptive activity group and, from the selected logistic model, an estimated probability of cardiovascular death over the NHANES follow-up with its 95% confidence interval.
The output is cohort-based context, not an individual diagnosis.
In two NHANES cohorts measured with different devices, we separated each participant's average day into a 24-hour cosinor rhythm and a residual shape.
The leading shape components were 12-hour and 8-hour patterns that the cosinor cannot represent, and activity profiles varied continuously between people rather than forming distinct phenotypes.
One shape component, FPC2, which contrasts an early-starting, flat day with a day with distinct morning and evening activity peaks, had the same shape in both cohorts.
It was associated with higher all-cause mortality in unweighted analyses in both cohorts.

The association was concentrated in cardiovascular deaths, which were associated with FPC2 in both cohorts with survey weights, and it was unchanged after excluding deaths in the first two years and after adjustment for additional rhythm metrics, activity volume and lifestyle factors.
FPC2 was not associated with cancer mortality.
Functional data generally contain both phase and amplitude, but traditional methods often ignore the phase part and model only amplitude, using techniques like FPCA [44].
text.formatted: Functional data generally contain both phase and amplitude, but traditional methods often ignore the phase part and model only amplitude, using techniques like FPCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[44]</ref>.

text.text: In our study, the decomposition into the cosinor fit and the residual curve is orthogonal, so the two cover non-overlapping parts of the daily profile.

Applying FPCA to the residuals yields shape components that do not overlap with the mean activity level, amplitude, and timing; in addition, multilevel FPCA [45] further distinguishes a participant's usual shape from day-to-day variation.
text.formatted: Applying FPCA to the residuals yields shape components that do not overlap with the mean activity level, amplitude, and timing; in addition, multilevel FPCA <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[45]</ref> further distinguishes a participant's usual shape from day-to-day variation.

text.text: The components of our approach, the cosinor model and functional data analysis, are well established [46]; our contribution lies in combining them so that the added value of the functional representation can be assessed directly and cleanly.
text.formatted: The components of our approach, the cosinor model and functional data analysis, are well established <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[46]</ref>; our contribution lies in combining them so that the added value of the functional representation can be assessed directly and cleanly.

text.text: Our results answer the question raised in the introduction.
Once the cosinor fit is removed, the remaining daily shape is dominated by two peaks that varies in its timing (FPC1) and prominence (FPC2).
Neither a single 24-hour cosine nor the extended cosinor can capture such multimodal, asymmetric shapes.
The low end of FPC2 resembles the bi-phasic profile described by Xiao et al. [10].
text.formatted: The low end of FPC2 resembles the bi-phasic profile described by Xiao et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: In our models, cosinor amplitude remained the strongest rhythm predictor of mortality, consistent with previous studies reporting associations between rest-activity amplitude and mortality [25, 26, 27].
text.formatted: In our models, cosinor amplitude remained the strongest rhythm predictor of mortality, consistent with previous studies reporting associations between rest-activity amplitude and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the 12-hour harmonic component (FPC2) was associated with cardiovascular but not all-cause mortality in the survey-weighted models.
A link between this structure and cardiovascular disease is biologically plausible.

Disrupted daily rest-activity rhythms were associated with higher mortality, cardiovascular disease and accelerated biological ageing [9, 43, 47], and 12-hour rhythms in gene expression and metabolism are coordinated by a cell-autonomous 12-hour clock distinct from the circadian clock [48].
text.formatted: Disrupted daily rest-activity rhythms were associated with higher mortality, cardiovascular disease and accelerated biological ageing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">47]</ref>, and 12-hour rhythms in gene expression and metabolism are coordinated by a cell-autonomous 12-hour clock distinct from the circadian clock <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[48]</ref>.

text.text: Cardiovascular physiology also has a 12-hour structure: blood pressure follows a bimodal daily course [49, 50, 51], and an exaggerated morning surge predicts stroke independently of 24-hour blood pressure [52].
text.formatted: Cardiovascular physiology also has a 12-hour structure: blood pressure follows a bimodal daily course <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">51]</ref>, and an exaggerated morning surge predicts stroke independently of 24-hour blood pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[52]</ref>.

text.text: The higher-risk end of FPC2 combines more activity at night, an earlier start, no mid-morning surge and less evening activity.
This pattern could arise from disrupted sleep or nocturnal activity, or from fewer periods of structured or discretionary activity during the day.

The cardiovascular association was not explained by income, mobility difficulty or activity volume, and it persisted after excluding early deaths, which argues against a simple explanation by illness-related inactivity.

Our study showed a robust association between the 12-hour component (FPC2) and cardiovascular mortality, suggesting that FPC2 may serve as an early behavioural marker of subclinical cardiovascular disease.
The association between FPC2 and mortality differed between the unweighted and surveyweighted Cox models.

The two models answer different questions [53]: the weighted model estimates the association averaged over the U.S. adult population, whereas the unweighted model estimates the association in the sampled cohort, conditional on the covariates included.
text.formatted: The two models answer different questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[53]</ref>: the weighted model estimates the association averaged over the U.S. adult population, whereas the unweighted model estimates the association in the sampled cohort, conditional on the covariates included.

text.text: NHANES oversamples older adults, who therefore account for most deaths while carrying relatively little survey weight.
Our results showed that survey weighting moved the all-cause and cardiovascular estimates in opposite directions.
These findings should be con-firmed in larger cohorts with more deaths, which would also allow age-stratified associations to be examined.

In addition, further adjustment for other potential confounders, such as weekday-weekend differences and shift work , could be considered in future analyses of the association between the proposed shape component and mortality.
Several studies have applied functional clustering to identify representative physical behaviour profiles [farrahi_data-driven_nodate, 54, 55].
text.formatted: Several studies have applied functional clustering to identify representative physical behaviour profiles [farrahi_data-driven_nodate, <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">55]</ref>.

text.text: In these studies, cluster validity was usually assessed by visual separation of cluster trajectories and by differences in health outcomes between clusters [19, 21].
text.formatted: In these studies, cluster validity was usually assessed by visual separation of cluster trajectories and by differences in health outcomes between clusters <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">21]</ref>.

text.text: In our data, activity profiles varied continuously between participants, with no clear cluster structure.
This is consistent with [21], who reported only small differences between clusters derived from 36 accelerometer metrics covering rest-activity rhythm, daytime activity, sleep and chronotype.
text.formatted: This is consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref>, who reported only small differences between clusters derived from 36 accelerometer metrics covering rest-activity rhythm, daytime activity, sleep and chronotype.

text.text: We therefore consider continuous component scores the appropriate predictors in health analyses, while clusters remain useful as descriptive profile types for communicating results, as in our web application.
The mortality prediction model in the interactive tool asks users for only a few personal details (age, sex and income category) in addition to their accelerometry data.
It still achieved a relatively high AUC while limiting the personal information users must share.
This study has several strengths.
The decomposition separates rhythm from shape by construction.
The analysis was replicated in an independent cohort with a different device placement and measurement unit, and the leading components had nearly identical shapes in both cohorts.
The findings were also robust to extensive covariate adjustment.
The study also has limitations.
Minutes without valid data were set to zero.
This mainly affected the hip cohort at night, when the device was removed, so the hip residual partly reflects device removal rather than activity.
In addition, hip counts and wrist MIMS capture different aspects of movement, so components with the same shape should be interpreted with caution across cohorts.
The within-day structure of activity that a 24-hour cosinor cannot represent varies continuously between people.
Its second leading component contrasts a day with distinct morning and evening activity peaks against an early-starting, flat day.

This component was associated with higher all-cause or cardiovascular mortality in two independent NHANES cohorts, independently of 24-hour rhythm strength, timing and activity volume, although the specific outcome depended on survey weighting.
These exploratory findings suggest that the shape of daily activity carries prognostic information beyond standard rhythm summaries.
